On 7 October 1958 the president of Pakistan scrapped the constitution, dismissed the government and declared martial law. Three weeks later the army chief, General Ayub Khan, sent the president into exile and took his place. It was the first of the army's takeovers.

Pakistan had begun badly. Jinnah died a year after independence and his deputy was shot in 1951. The country took nine years to write a constitution and went through seven prime ministers in eleven. Officials and generals from the west of the country did not want an election, because the Bengalis of the east were the majority.

Ayub ruled for more than ten years. He allied Pakistan closely with the United States, built a new capital at Islamabad, signed the Indus Waters Treaty and brought in a law limiting polygamy. Industry grew quickly, and the gains went to a few families and mostly to the west. He let only 80,000 local councillors vote for the president.

The war of 1965 broke his standing. Protests forced him out in 1969, and he handed power to another general, under whom the country split (see the war of 1971).

The army ruled Pakistan directly again from 1977 to 1988 (see Zia-ul-Haq) and from 1999 to 2008.
